articles.title: Russia is escalating its attacks on Europe. The risk of a misstep is growing every day
articles.summary: It is a strategy built around a contradiction. Russia’s attacks on Europe aim to make war feel closer, without starting it. To provoke, without forcing a res...
articles.body:
It is a strategy built around a contradiction. Russia's attacks on Europe aim to make war feel closer, without starting it. To provoke, without forcing a response. To alarm, without causing a real change in behavior.

Moscow has palpably escalated its "grey-zone" conflict with NATO in Europe in the past week. Since late Sunday, a railway on which top former Western officials were traveling has been attacked by a Russian drone, another drone of likely Russian origin has been shot down in Lithuania, a third has washed up on Polish shores, a Danish helicopter has narrowly been missed by a Russian flare, and Dutch trains have been paralyzed by an as-yet unclaimed act of sabotage.

None of this is by accident. And it comes after weeks of warnings Moscow would seek to escalate with NATO – but perhaps not because it seeks or can afford a full-on conflict with the largest military alliance in history.

Instead, Russian President Vladimir Putin , has two goals, expedited by a Trump administration loathed to upset him having half a term left, and Ukraine's air defenses being in a woefully undersupplied state.

First is to make the cost of supporting Ukraine feel real and growing, and weigh on the minds of European voters, as pro-Russian right-wing parties vie for electoral power in several countries in the region. The second is to test Article 5 – the bedrock of the NATO alliance, in which an attack on one member is an attack on all, and Putin's long-term bugbear. Be in no doubt, Russia is getting away with sabotage, border violations and assassination plots that in the Cold War would have sparked existential angst. Now it seems commonplace.

As one European diplomat told me: "What's happening now would have triggered NATO's Article 4 just a few months ago," referring to the clause in the alliance's treaty calling for an emergency meeting over a crisis. "Now, it's becoming almost a daily occurrence." Speaking on the condition of anonymity for discussing a sensitive matter, the diplomat added Russia's goal was "to scare Europe away from supporting Ukraine," and "play with the fear of escalation."

NATO's major problem is that this is likely not the peak of Russian malice, but opening salvos.

A peace deal seems more than distant, with the United States ineffective in its pressure, and Putin clearly set on the goal of taking the eastern Donbas region , then perhaps more of Ukraine. And while Russia's horrific squandering of human capital in frontline "meat wave" infantry attacks somewhat curbs its ambitions, the Kremlin's military-industrial complex is providing new, real options: a cheap and highly effective form of air power its adversaries struggle to defeat, and which it can increasingly mass-produce.

Russia's Geran 4 and 5 drones are powered by Chinese-made turbojet engines, which cost about $40,000, according to Ukrainian officials and media reports, with each device retailing at about $70,000. Their Banderol cruise missile can reach speeds of 375 mph, and may reportedly cost as little as $100,000. Anything these weapons lack in polish or accuracy is made up for in sheer volume. And again, Moscow is just getting started, with its Alabuga drone factory adapting fast to flood the front lines and beyond with this new threat.

Production is key. Dr. Marina Miron, from the Defence Studies Department at King's College London, said that "adaptation when it comes to production, supply chains, logistics, doctrine" was a vital part of any strategy, even if it grabbed less headlines than the integration of AI into Ukraine and Russia's battlefield reconnaissance and attack. "And both sides are trying to adapt and innovate, to benefit from a short window… while the adversary designs countermeasures" to stop the new advances, she told me.

"NATO is well behind when it comes to readiness to deal with these changes," Miron added. "It is not just about building drone defenses… [but] about rethinking the entire doctrine." She said ideally NATO would not copy Ukraine or Russia, but adapt to "the lessons from both sides."

Miron said the probability of conventional war was "low," but what NATO would instead "be facing are 'events' below threshold as we have witnessed in Poland, Romania, Denmark, etc."

In this brewing crisis, part of the challenge for NATO members is how to convey to its public the gravity of the threat they are now continually facing, without causing panic and granting a psychological win to Moscow. It is a near-impossible needle to thread. A near-miss drone attack at a German airport, a ballistic missile landing in open-ground in Poland, assassination plots alleged in indictments filed in New York's Southern District. The list grows from the late summer, as does its potential lethality and geographical spread.

Moscow may be better suited to this sort of precarious dance. A senior European official said the Russian mindset was better adjusted than NATO's to erratic escalation. "The Russians have since Soviet times theorized the flexible adjustment of power and aggression," he noted. " For NATO, escalation management in this way is more of a new thing. So there are things for NATO to learn."

He added: "Overreaction is not useful, but turning the other cheek is not either."

At some point, Moscow will misfire, overstep and oblige a NATO member to respond with force in some way. It is not unprecedented: In Syria, a 2018 attack on US positions by Russian Wagner mercenaries drew a ferocious US military response. We should also not forget that European NATO arms and intelligence are assisting Ukraine daily to hit Russia. This is often weaponry bought and supplied by NATO, but with Ukrainians pressing the trigger. Moscow – in its warped perspective as the invader – perhaps feels as though it is pushing back.

But when Russia's misstep occurs, the jump-step in confrontation that it will bring is one NATO's military and public are not ready for. It is likely closer by the day.

articles.title: As price of fuel ratchets up, so does anger of people who can no longer afford it
articles.summary: Protesters are taking to the streets around the world to voice anger about skyrocketing fuel prices and rolling blackouts, as the now monthslong US war with...
articles.body:
Protesters are taking to the streets around the world to voice anger about skyrocketing fuel prices and rolling blackouts, as the now monthslong US war with Iran drives up the cost of energy globally.

Oil prices climbed back above the $100 per barrel mark last week in the wake of further US strikes on Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf and reignited fighting in Yemen that threatens shipping in the Bab al-Mandab Strait .

For the United States, that has meant elevated gas prices and stark warnings for households that rely on heating oil to keep warm in the winter, as analysts forecast a 30% jump in prices amid the Iran war.

For less wealthy nations, the hit to their national finances – and people's wallets – has been even starker with patience often running out.

As the price of fuel ratchets up, so does the anger of people who can no longer afford to pay for gas, get to work, run their businesses or even carry out essential services.

Governments are also scrambling to respond to the economic fallout. In Pakistan, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Thursday approved a nationwide austerity and energy conservation campaign in response to rising global petroleum prices linked to tensions in the Middle East, according to a statement from the Prime Minister's Office.

The measures include a 50% reduction in fuel allocations for government vehicles for three months, with exemptions for ambulances, fire services, law enforcement agencies and vehicles used for other essential services.

In Syria, protesters burned tires on a busy highway. In Guatemala, they blocked roads to demand immediate government action. And in Portugal, local business leaders and workers marched to the prime minister's home.

Here's a closer look at the protests and the global impacts of sky-high energy costs:

A steep rise in fuel prices over the weekend ignited protests across Syria, marking the largest demonstrations in the country since the fall of the Assad regime two years ago.

The country's government temporarily raised diesel prices to 175 Syrian pounds ($1.43) a liter – roughly a 40% hike – according to Syrian news agency SANA. It also raised prices for gas by more than 25%.

The Syrian Energy Ministry has said the steep price increases are due to surging global fuel prices and ongoing maintenance at the country's largest refinery, Baniyas, which has increased its reliance on imports, SANA reported.

While dozens of protests have been peaceful, demonstrators on Sunday blocked the Hasaka–Deir ez-Zor highway, where they burned tires and stopped oil tankers, according to ACLED , a global conflict monitor.

"Fuel availability, rising prices, falling purchasing power, and poor services are all reasons that have accumulated public resentment, although demands are also shifting toward reversing decisions and removing officials, including the energy minister, showing that economic grievances are turning into grievances against the government," said Muaz Al Abdullah, a Syria analyst at ACLED.

Video filmed by Reuters news agency from the scene of a protest in Aleppo on Sunday shows people burning tires and shouting chants criticizing the governments' fuel hike decision.

"All those present here want a reduction in diesel prices. We don't want higher wages, we want cheaper (fuel)," one Syrian protester, Yasser Salim, told Reuters.

Another protester, Bassam al-Ali, said: "We do not want roundabouts, every day they (the government) build a new roundabout that costs a million thousand dollars, and malls and I don't know what … Your people were with you, is still with you now and will remain with you – but this will let things explode."

Last week in Guatemala, groups of organized truckers and other protesters blocked highways and caused damage in various parts of the country to protest rising fuel prices, according to the Associated Press .

Other videos taken by local media show people marching peacefully through Guatemala City to demand immediate government action.

The country's Congress is now working to address the widespread discontent through a proposed law that would cap prices until the end of the year, but the bill is still making its way through the legislative process, according to Guatemala's national news agency AGN. If passed, it would mean that a government subsidy is paid to fuel importers if prices exceed the established cap, according to AP.

"This is an issue that must be resolved as a country. The executive, the legislative, and everyone else involved must resolve it. People cannot pay these prices and not feel the impact on their finances," said the president of the Congress, Luis Contreras Colindres, in an address on Monday.

"Diesel is the engine that drives this country's economy," Contreras said, according to AGN .

Protests took place in the coastal city of Espinho, Portugal, on Saturday to protest both rising gas prices and the soaring cost of living.

About 80 people took part in that demonstration, which was organized by local business leaders and aimed at pressuring the government to find solutions, according to Portugal's Lusa News Agency. The protesters marched until they reached the home of Prime Minister Luís Montenegro in Espinho.

Meanwhile, the Portuguese Firefighters' League (LBP) has sounded the alarm that surging fuel prices are becoming unsustainable for fire brigades and saddling volunteer organizations with costs they can't keep up with.

On Monday, the country's government announced a new package of measures intended to ease the fuel price crunch, according to Lusa. Those measures include support for freight transporters, taxi drivers, the fire service and the social sector, the news agency reported.

About 50 fishermen blockaded a major fuel depot in the coastal southern French town of Fos-sur-Mer on Tuesday, in part to protest rising fuel prices, according to CNN affiliate BFMTV.

The blockade lasted several hours and the protesters briefly clashed with police, BFMTV reported.

Mayor Philippe Maurizot said the fishing industry in the town is facing a "profound crisis that demands an urgent and strong response from the state," and said the protesters' anger "must be heard."

"Rising costs, increased fuel prices, a growing number of constraints, insufficient income, and a lack of visibility are placing some professionals in an untenable situation," he said in the letter addressed to the French prime minister.

Workers of the Philippine transport group Manibela went on strike on Monday to protest fuel price hikes – calling for government subsidies and scrapped fuel taxes.

It comes as petroleum companies in the country announced another round of fuel price hikes, which went into effect on Tuesday, hitting drivers with an increase of 5.68 pesos (0.01) per liter of gas, according to the Philippine News Agency (PNA). The prices of diesel and kerosene were also hiked again this week, according to PNA.

"We know that every increase at the pump affects more than the cost of filling up a vehicle. It affects the daily budget of families, the livelihood of our drivers, and the operating costs of businesses," said Energy Secretary Energy Secretary Sharon S. Garin, as she announced on Tuesday that the government had cleared a hurdle to potentially reduce excise taxes on petroleum products.

Bus drivers and motorists have been struggling for months amid the rising costs, which surged drastically in March and still remain elevated compared to pre-war prices.

Back in March at the height of the country's fuel crisis – about a month after the start of the Iran war – people in Manila marched toward the country's presidential palace to express discontent with steeply rising energy prices.

"The Philippines should stand up and call for an end to the US aggression against Iran. The impact of the oil disruption affects us all. We might not have been hit by bombs, but we are being hit by poverty and hunger because of the rise in oil prices," said trade union leader Jerome Adonis in late March.

Student unions have also joined the widespread protests at various points this year, railing against a wider cost of living crisis in the Philippines.

CNN's Heather Law and Sophia Saifi contributed to this report.

articles.title: Judge orders Trump to give 30 days notice before any steps to demolish Kennedy Center
articles.summary: WASHINGTON, Sept 17 (Reuters) - A federal judge ordered President Donald Trump's administration on Thursday to provide at least 30 days' notice before taking...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, Sept 17 (Reuters) - A federal judge ordered President Donald Trump's administration on Thursday to provide at least 30 days' notice before taking any steps to demolish the Kennedy Center, the landmark performing arts venue ‌that has become a flashpoint in his efforts to reshape the U.S. capital.

U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper issued the order after ‌lawyers for a Democratic congresswoman who is suing to keep the venue open and Trump's name off its facade submitted new evidence citing the Republican president's comments on Wednesday referring ​to demolishing the Kennedy Center.

"I think that the Trump administration should certainly have recognition. Because frankly, if we don't do that, it's going to close. It'll end up being ripped down," Trump told reporters in North Carolina, referring to putting his name on the facility established by Congress and opened in 1971 as a memorial to slain President John Kennedy.

Matt Floca, the Kennedy Center's Trump-backed executive director, said in a court filing earlier on Thursday that ‌the building was being temporarily closed to assess safety ⁠risks in areas "exhibiting severe structural deterioration."

Democratic U.S. Representative Joyce Beatty, who sued Trump last year over his Kennedy Center plans, responded in a filing in federal court in Washington that the closure "is a recipe for defendants extending their ⁠shutdown forever and closing the Kennedy Center for the next two years — the very thing this court said they could not do without its permission."

Beatty's lawyers also cited a photo circulating on social media that depicted the president aboard Air Force One looking at a poster they said appeared to be titled "Kennedy ​Center ​DEMOLISHED." The photo has not been independently verified by Reuters.

Trump last year had the ​White House's historic East Wing demolished to make way for ‌a ballroom project he has pursued.

Cooper turned down a request by Beatty for an emergency hearing on her lawsuit after the Kennedy Center's board, including Trump and his hand-picked appointees, voted this week to close the venue for up to two years for a $257 million renovation project.

Beatty, an ex officio member of the Kennedy Center's board, said the venue is no longer accessible to the public during normal operating hours. New barriers were visible outside the building on Wednesday.

Beatty and other critics have accused Trump of seeking to place his name on the Kennedy ‌Center out of vanity. Trump's name had been placed on the building's facade ​until the judge in May ordered it removed, saying only Congress can change the ​name.

Cooper earlier directed the board to explain by Thursday whether the administration's ​plan violates an earlier order he issued limiting its ability to shut its doors. The board said on ‌Thursday morning that it was not in violation of the ​order, and the seven-day emergency closure ​was separate from the larger renovation plans.

The Trump administration said it would ask the judge by Friday to dissolve the prior order to allow for what the government called "closure necessary to complete the restoration and renovations."

Cooper, in a ruling on Tuesday, rejected the center's latest ​effort to put Trump's name on the building ‌to reflect his role in the planned renovation. The administration has appealed, and Trump said on social media the Kennedy ​Center "is destined to doom" if it is not permitted to close for repairs.

(Reporting by Katharine Jackson and Mike Scarcella; Editing ​by Will Dunham, Doina Chiacu, Andrea Ricci, David Bario and Rod Nickel)

articles.title: Como filhote encontrado por acaso ajudou a desvendar nova espécie | G1
articles.standfirst: Animal encontrado por um morador em 2016 ajudou cientistas a reconhecer uma linhagem até então não descrita pela ciência; descoberta foi liderada por pesquisador da PUCRS.
articles.summary: Animal encontrado por um morador em 2016 ajudou cientistas a reconhecer uma linhagem até então não descrita pela ciência; descoberta foi liderada por pesquisador da PUCRS.
articles.body:
A descoberta da primeira nova espécie de felino atual descrita pela ciência em mais de 100 anos teve início em 2016, quando um filhote encontrado por um morador nas montanhas da Bolívia chamou a atenção de pesquisadores.

Em 2016, um morador de Nor Yungas encontrou um filhote de gato selvagem e o encaminhou ao refúgio de animais La Senda Verde. À primeira vista, o animal parecia pertencer a uma espécie já conhecida pelos pesquisadores. No entanto, análises genéticas realizadas posteriormente mostraram que o filhote não fazia parte da espécie à qual havia sido associado inicialmente, a Leopardus tigrinus .

Os resultados apontaram que ele integrava uma linhagem própria, desconhecida até então pelos cientistas.

Foi a partir dessa constatação que pesquisadores liderados pelo professor Eduardo Eizirikda, da Pontifícia Universidade Católica do Rio Grande do Sul (PUCRS), descreveram uma nova espécie de felino selvagem, batizada de Leopardus tilcayo .

Professor de universidade do RS descobre nova espécie de felino selvagem — Foto: Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz

Segundo os cientistas, espécies desse grupo apresentam aparência muito semelhante entre si , o que contribuiu para que animais geneticamente distintos fossem classificados como uma única espécie durante décadas .

Apesar da semelhança, os estudos indicam que algumas dessas populações seguem trajetórias evolutivas independentes há centenas de milhares ou até milhões de anos.

"Essa semelhança visual fez com que diferentes espécies fossem, durante muito tempo, confundidas e classificadas como uma só", afirma o professor.

Os resultados, publicados na revista científica Current Biology, também trouxeram uma nova compreensão sobre a diversidade dos gatos-do-mato da América do Sul.

Para Eizirik, o caso mostra que a biodiversidade ainda guarda surpresas, inclusive entre animais considerados conhecidos pela ciência.

"Este é um estudo que evidencia o quanto ainda há para se descobrir sobre a biodiversidade do planeta. Mesmo entre animais carismáticos e conhecidos como os felinos, espécies podem permanecer desconhecidas durante séculos", diz Eizirik.

articles.title: Drone attacks by Colombian armed groups more than double in early 2026
articles.summary: Civilians are caught in the crossfire of drone attacks between armed groups and government forces.
articles.body:
Drone attacks by armed groups in Colombia surged 146 percent in the first five months of this year compared with the same period in 2025, according to the country’s Ombudsman’s Office.

The attacks killed 21 people and wounded 145 others, including children. Civilians accounted for nearly a third of those killed or wounded, the office said on Thursday.

Ombudsman Iris Marin warned that the drones inflict fear well beyond the immediate casualties, with their recurring buzz terrorising communities in conflict-affected areas.

Drones are part of the escalating war between armed groups and government forces, leaving civilians caught in between.

Homes, educational institutions, petrol stations and infrastructure were also hit.

Marin said that in some territories, fear of overflights and attacks has also triggered displacements, restrictions on mobility, and difficulties in working the fields, accessing health centres or carrying out daily activities.

It is common in the country for armed groups to demonstrate their strength using lethal, makeshift drones rigged with explosives.

The Ombudsman said the attacks have “restricted access for humanitarian missions and hindered processes of return and permanence in the territories”.

Analysts have said armed groups use the aerial devices for two main purposes: attacks and surveillance. They target and launch attacks on rival groups as well as state forces , and survey illegal coca fields.

Last month, a Human Rights Watch report said children are being trained in drone warfare. The watchdog also said that armed groups are recruiting children through social media platforms like Meta and TikTok.

The flight of unmanned aircraft over Colombia’s rugged terrain makes neutralising them difficult.

In January 2026, the Colombian government announced a $1.68bn project to develop an anti-drone shield.

Colombia’s right-wing president, Abelardo de la Espriella, governs from a military stronghold in Barranquilla and is waging a frontal offensive against armed groups with support from the United States. Recent operations by Colombian troops have utilised US-made drones, a military source told AFP.

In recent months, Colombian military forces have also used grenade-launching drones to counter armed fighters.

articles.body: The Archbishop of Canterbury's office has withdrawn an interfaith award given to a Muslim cleric after past comments surfaced in which he praised Osama bin Laden. Maulana Hafiz Muhammad Tahir Mehmood Ashrafi received the Hubert Walter Award for Reconciliation and Interfaith Cooperation at Lambeth Palace last Friday, during a ceremony that coincided with the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks. Lambeth Palace announced the reversal Thursday after previous comments by Ashrafi had "come to light," causing it to reconsider the award. "It is a longstanding principle of interfaith dialogue and co-operation that we must engage with one another across deeply-held differences, and that remains the case," Lambeth Palace said in a statement. Lambeth Palace added that it continues "to pray for the Christian community in Pakistan, and for all those working for interfaith dialogue and harmony in Pakistan and around the world." SEAL WHO KILLED BIN LADEN RECALLS 9/11 MOMENT THAT CHANGED HIS LIFE: ‘WELCOME TO MY WORLD’ According to the BBC, Ashrafi said in 2007 that bin Laden — the architect of the 9/11 attacks — had "been fighting for Islam against the Russians, Americans and British." articles.title: The lost Corsair: The search for a Korean War legend and its missing pilot
articles.summary: US Navy and Marine Corps pilots called the F4U Corsair the “The Widowmaker.”
articles.body: US Navy and Marine Corps pilots called the F4U Corsair the “The Widowmaker.” Not because it was responsible for shooting down more than 2,100 Japanese planes in World War II, but because it was tricky to handle; so powerful that if its pilot adjusted the throttle too quickly the torque from its 18-cylinder engine could flip it over and send it crashing, upside down, into the sea. Japanese ground troops called it “Whistling Death,” for the sound it made during bombing and strafing runs, a role that would become even more important during the 1950-53 Korean War. In Korea, 494 Corsairs would be lost, including one flying off the aircraft carrier USS Essex on February 21, 1952. It was never seen again. Until, maybe, now. Mystery find Scuba diver Kim Kyung-soo has 25 years’ experience in the waters off Korea and elsewhere. But what he saw one day in May 2025 was a mystery to him. Leading a group of divers into the waters off Yangyang, South Korea, Kim dropped anchor at a well-explored diving spot. But a strong tidal current pushed the anchor into even deeper waters, he told CNN. “When we reached 45 meters (148 feet) depth, I couldn’t see the seafloor. I was swimming around in that depth when I saw a dark object on the floor,” Kim recalled. “I couldn’t see the exact shape, but it had a long cylindrical form like a submarine. Not too big though… I thought it could be a small submarine from North Korea.” Kim was curious. But the object was at least another seven meters (23 feet) below him, and a deeper descent was too much of a risk for his inexperienced students. So, he left his curiosity behind with the unknown object in the water. A gray, frigid Thursday Carrier Air Group Five was operating off the east coast of Korea that Thursday in February ’52, flying off four aircraft carriers – USS Valley Forge, USS Antietam, USS Philippine Sea and the Essex. The air group had been on station just a few days when combat orders came in for February 21. It would launch 85 combat sorties, flying close-air support for ground troops and photo reconnaissance, as well as strikes against enemy supply lines and installations. It was cold and snowy, but combat reports show the planes of Carrier Air Group Five made an impact that day: “The Air Group cut railroad tracks in 33 places, 6 trucks were destroyed, 11 buildings destroyed, 1 barracks burned, 25 railroad cars destroyed and 25 were damaged.” The price to the US Pacific Fleet was two aircraft lost. That afternoon, an AD-4 sustained battle damage. The Essex sent out help, a Corsair to escort the Skyraider back to the carrier. But the weather was as much an enemy as the North Koreans or the Chinese. An “F4U crashed into the sea shortly after entering a snow storm while escorting a battle-damaged AD,” Pacific Fleet records state. “Probable cause, pilot … disoriented in snowstorm. Not recovered; listed as killed in the line of duty,” a report from the Essex’s commanding officer states. A new clue “Usually when you tell people you saw something (underwater) they don’t believe you. They say, ‘Don’t lie! You must be mistaken,’” Kim, the scuba diver, said. But one of Kim’s students, An Hyun-jin, listened, believed and searched. And searched. And searched. An, who owns a dive shop and has been diving for more than five years, would go back under the waves looking for what Kim saw more than 10 times until … “When I found the propeller, I was really surprised that Kim was not wrong about seeing something; like wow, there really is a plane, and my heart started beating fast,” An told CNN. But it took a while longer to find that mysterious cylinder, which would turn out to be the forward fuselage of a plane. They got close and, without touching the aircraft, moved the sediment to reveal the distinctive inverted gull-shaped wings, leading them to believe it was a Corsair. Kim knew the significance of preserving and documenting such findings, having participated in several recovery works with nonprofit organization Global Underwater Explorers in Europe, and the South Korean government at Chosei Coal Mine in Japan’s Yamaguchi prefecture, where more than 130 Koreans were killed in 1942, during the Japanese colonial period. He led an 11-person crew diving to the site, armed with devices for measuring the wreckage and rendering it into a three-dimensional model. Photographic evidence In photos and videos captured by the divers and seen by CNN, the plane appears embedded in the seafloor, rusted and covered in barnacles, as could be expected after decades under water. The tail had been torn away and is nowhere to be seen. There’s no propeller or cockpit canopy. But it has the profile of a Corsair, its distinctive wings and long nose that covered that powerful engine offering clear indicators of the model, according to a CNN comparison of the pictures alongside historical photos and blueprints. As they made those photos last year, the divers knew they were on to something. They shared their findings with South Korea’s defense agency for recovery and identification, one of only two government agencies in the world dedicated to identifying those killed in action. Impressed with the divers’ find, the South Koreans shared the detailed documentation of the plane with their American counterparts at the Hawaii-based Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency (DPAA), who were aware of a Corsair that crashed into the water after returning from combat action in 1952, and the pilot never heard from again. In short order, the Yangyang mission became a priority for the Americans. Underwater archaeology The sun beat down on the rigid-hulled rubber boat as Meghan Mumford stood tall over the other five people aboard. An underwater forensic archaeologist, she scanned the sea, trying to pinpoint the best spot to drop an underwater drone, whose sensors could help confirm Kim’s find. Mumford felt the weight and responsibility of her job. “I think it’s truly an honor to bring answers and repatriate our servicemembers and our heroes not only to our nation but specifically to their families,” she said. The DPAA says 7,354 Americans are still missing from the Korean War, among more than 80,000 from all actions since World War II. Multiple thousands of descendants and relatives are still waiting for answers. DPAA goes wherever it has credible evidence and a chance of providing relatives with closure, juggling searches in 46 countries to try to put resources where they’ll have the best chance of finding identifiable remains. The Yangyang site fits the bill. Locating and recovering remains require a long process, starting with interviewing local residents or witnesses, digging through historical records, and carefully excavating bones and artifacts for DNA analysis at the agency’s Hawaii lab before returning them to the remaining relatives. DPAA team leader Spencer Jefferson, a US Army captain, told CNN that the agency wouldn’t notify families that remains have been found until bone tissue has been found and tested at its own lab. “From there, we can positively identify who exactly this is,” he said. Mission in Yangyang The weather was “oddly calm,” noted Commanding Officer Choi Seong-woo when CNN joined DPAA and its South Korean counterpart in August on their mission to verify the Yangyang wreckage. After sailing about half an hour, Choi’s navy yard utility boat slowed and hovered – never fully stopping as the water was far deeper than the length of the anchor. Fishing nets were obstacles for Mumford’s team as they tried to scan the ocean floor with two underwater drones. Once the drones were safely in the water, the team spent five hours scanning the sea floor – and confirmed there was indeed an aircraft below them. Black sheep and angels Team leader Spencer agreed that, based on the photos taken by the divers, the wreckage has all the signs of being a Corsair. “This has the potential of being something we’re looking for … the shape, and the different engine compartments and things like that,” he said. Corsairs entered service in 1942, and more than 12,500 were delivered to the US military by 1952. While the F4U was designed to be operated off carriers, in its early years the US military had trouble figuring out how to do that in practice, according to the National World War II Museum in New Orleans. So, it made its mark flying off airstrips on Pacific islands, in air-to-air combat but also as a fighter-bomber in battles over Guadalcanal and the Solomons, the museum says. It also notes the most heralded operators of the Corsair, Marine Fighting Squadron 214, also known as the “Black Sheep Squadron.” The unit – cobbled together from pilots without units – shot down or destroyed more than 200 Japanese planes from August 1943 to January 1944. Its exploits inspired the 1970s TV series “Black Sheep Squadron,” bringing new fame to the Corsair. Those victories flying off island airstrips might have been the final legacy of the Corsair, but British Royal Navy pilots figured out how to fly it off carriers, according to the museum. It would be incorporated into the US carrier fleet by 1944, and in the 1945 Battle of Okinawa, Corsair pilots were instrumental in blunting Japanese kamikaze attacks on American warships, earning the nickname “Angels of Okinawa,” the museum says. One of the “Sseksseki” Koreans didn’t have a specific name for the Corsair. US fighter planes were called “Sseksseki” for the sound they made zooming by. But the Corsair was still a force on the war. In the first 10 months of combat, 82% of ground-support missions were flown by Corsairs, according to the Vought Heritage Foundation. The pilot on one of those missions, flown during the frigid Battle of the Chosin Reservoir in late 1950, recalled the action in a 2000 essay for the US Naval Institute’s Naval History magazine. Marine pilot Lyle Bradley and a wingman were tasked with supporting the 15,000 men of the First Marine Division, who were surrounded by several Chinese divisions. Checking in by radio with a Marine air controller on the ground, codenamed Dunkirk 1-4, the Corsair pilots heard their importance. “We are happy to see you Corsairs. Please circle us as long as possible. You’re our link to the outside world,” Bradley quotes the controller as saying. He would go on to give the American pilot instructions on where to hit the Chinese, and Bradley released 2,000 pounds of bombs on the target. “Looks like a perfect hit,” Dunkirk 1-4 said. “We love you Corsair people.” Attending a history conference in Wyoming almost 40 years later, Bradley writes, he came across the Marine air controller who was Dunkirk 1-4. “He hugged me and exclaimed, ‘You guys saved our fannies!’” Once in the family It’s said that once you’re in the military, you gain a whole new family. And the family you leave behind when you deploy is part of that greater new family. That’s why the aircraft wreckage at the bottom of the sea off the coast of Korea still matters. Families are key to the DPAA’s mission. DPAA personnel expect to be back off Yangyang in the near future. If there’s a chance the remains of that pilot are there, DPAA will keep looking. “Somewhere beneath a modern city, on a mountain, in the middle of a minefield, or in the deep seas may lie the last trace of a life cut short by war,” says Chris Jo, the Korea liaison officer of DPAA. “Fulfilling our nation’s promise is to leave no one behind and bring long-awaited closure to the families.”

articles.title: Empty podiums, prizes for e-voting, no opposition: Russians head to the polls amid intensifying war in Ukraine
articles.summary: Russia is holding parliamentary elections, the first since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, in a landscape in which critical opposition is effectively nonexistent.
articles.body: “The candidates have not shown up at our studio, so I’ll say goodbye for now,” Elizaveta Dorokhina, a Russia-1 state TV anchor, told viewers, with three empty podiums visible either side of her in the studio. The broadcast switched to a commercial break. All six registered candidates in Ryazan, a city 122 miles southeast of the Russian capital, had failed to turn up for a televised debate ahead of upcoming elections. Russia is holding parliamentary elections, the first since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, in a political landscape in which critical opposition is effectively nonexistent, with opponents barred or having fled the country. Voters will elect 450 members of the State Duma – the lower house of the Russian parliament – as well as regional and municipal heads. The empty studio offers a window into the democratic ritual Russia is so keen to put on display: the candidates, the debates, the appearance of choice. Projecting stability and an image of due processes has become a cornerstone of President Vladimir Putin’s Russia. The voting will take place over a three-day period starting Friday. The United Russia party, which backs Putin and has dominated domestic Russian politics for over 20 years, is widely expected to win a majority of seats. Among the areas voting are Russian-controlled parts of Ukraine – in Crimea, Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia. Russia’s only registered anti-war party, Yabloko – “apple” in Russian – was briefly allowed to take part before being barred by the Supreme Court last month. Grigory Yavlinsky, a co-founder of Yabloko and a prominent liberal Russian politician, told CNN that the Kremlin was taken aback by support for the party and its core message calling for a ceasefire in Ukraine. ‘Those who oppose are outcasts and enemies’ Although Putin is not on the ballot himself, Russia’s leader of more than two decades casts a long shadow over its politics. “The Russian political system is a rigid, personalistic regime with institutions that are imitational,” Andrei Kolesnikov, a Moscow-based political analyst and columnist for The New Times and Novaya Gazeta, told CNN. “Elections have no impact whatsoever on the nature of policy, which is predetermined. Their main purpose is to demonstrate to the public the ‘majority effect’: everyone is ‘for’ Putin’s policies, and those who oppose them are outcasts and enemies,” Kolesnikov added, who’s been labeled a “foreign agent” by Russian authorities. The vote is taking place amid a backdrop of creeping social tensions in Russia, as the Kremlin continues to propagate a war in Ukraine – now in its fifth year. Internet restrictions and a crackdown on civil society and dissent are impacting many Russians, even as Ukraine’s long-range strikes bring the war home to them in a new way. Kyiv’s drone attacks deep into Russian territory, designed to push the Kremlin into negotiations, have shattered the illusion that the consequences of what Moscow calls the “special military operation” are far removed from ordinary Russians. Some have resulted in loss of life and injuries (although nowhere near on the scale seen in Ukraine), but crucially, strikes on the country’s oil refineries have led to widespread fuel shortages, with queues of cars forming in major cities, while hits on Russia’s largest online retailers have increased pressure on the already strained wartime economy. That apprehension was reflected in the mood of voters in Moscow on a cold, crisp September day a week before the elections. Raisa, a voter in Moscow who, like everyone CNN spoke with, declined to give her full name, said she wanted “worthy people” elected who would “think about simple people” and their needs. When asked what she hopes the future will be like, she said, “I’d probably say what many people would: peaceful. I really want it all to end,” delicately nodding to the war. Marina Alexandrovna, 73, told CNN she was undecided who to vote for but that she “always votes,” adding: “It’s not who votes that matters, but who counts the votes.” Regarding the current political climate in Russia, “we know what life is, what laws are being passed. I don’t like it, but there’s nothing we can change,” she said. Authorities in Moscow have introduced material incentives for residents of the capital in the form of points for prizes, if they vote either online or at an electronic voting terminal at a polling station, rather than casting a paper ballot. Critics have long been suspicious of the Kremlin’s introduction of electronic voting because they argue it’s less transparent. A key distinction of these elections is that 186 veterans of the war in Ukraine are standing as candidates for State Duma, with more than 1,500 former servicemen also running for regional and municipal positions. This follows the launch of the “Time of Heroes” program by Putin in 2024 to train battle-hardened veterans for government and public servant roles. None of the war veteran candidates to whom CNN reached out wished to be interviewed. Only anti-war party barred from standing Arguably, who has been excluded from the ballot says more than the candidates who are allowed to participate. Yabloko was struck off only days after being registered for the election after a pro-Kremlin nationalist party, Rodina (Motherland in Russian), brought a lawsuit against the party alleging foreign financing and copyright violations. Yabloko’s leadership argues the move was politically motivated. At the party’s headquarters in Moscow, a running counter records the number of days that have passed since Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, next to a copy of a painting showing a pyramid of human skulls beneath circling crows by Vasily Vereshchagin. The 19th-century Russian painter became famous for his depictions of the horror of war. The image feels like a private memorial to Russia’s quashed anti-war movement. The Kremlin’s decision originally to allow Yabloko to stand in the parliamentary elections was a “low-risk experiment,” said Irina Busygina, a Russian political scientist now based in Berlin. Busygina believes once the Kremlin’s political operators saw a spike in online interest in Yabloko, with its calls for a peace deal with Ukraine, especially among the younger generations, they moved to neutralize the party, which had registered hundreds of candidates across the country. “(Putin) was not prepared for the situation where a liberal democratic party like Yabloko would have such strong support in the country,” co-founder Yavlinsky said. “We have no democracy in Russia yet. We started our reforms 30 years ago but failed completely, and that’s why we have an authoritarian system which is not prepared for democratic elections.” Yavlinsky added that those who are allowed to run in the elections are “100% supporting the current political line of the Kremlin,” whereas Yabloko is an opponent calling “for an alternative, to move to immediate ceasefire and negotiations with Ukraine, Europe, and with the United States.” Yavlinsky, who has spent 35 years in Russian politics, doesn’t expect any surprises in these elections, but said he hoped Russia would start diplomatic negotiations urgently. Moscow must “find common language with Europe, with Ukraine, with the US, because it’s the only way forward. It is necessary to avoid the possibility of nuclear war,” he said. Observers may question the point of holding elections where no meaningful opposition is allowed and the result appears largely predetermined. Russia has long criticized Ukraine’s lack of war-time elections, going so far as to refer to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky as “illegitimate” because he has outstayed his term and not called an election. Zelensky says holding elections while Ukraine is embroiled in the war is “impossible.” Ukraine’s constitution bars elections from being held under martial law, which was introduced after Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. Experts agree overwhelmingly the election results will be used to strengthen Putin’s mandate during war time. Russian social media channels have been rife with rumors of a further mobilization post-elections to shore up Russia’s manpower in Ukraine – something the Kremlin vehemently denies. According to Kolesnikov, “the elections will be presented as further legitimization of the special (military) operation and of the most brutal internal political repression and restrictions on citizens’ rights, which are now far more severe than anything seen in the late Soviet era.” But on the streets of Moscow, some remain optimistic that the future will be brighter. Sixty-three-year-old Oleg said he hoped “some stability will emerge for ordinary people… and that, going forward, our ties with good people abroad will improve. In both the West and the East.” Putin’s continued emphasis on addressing the war’s “root causes” and achieving his original goals – including demilitarizing and subjugating Ukraine – suggests that may be a long way off.

articles.title: Belfast duo go from 'fish out of water' to a Big Deal
articles.summary: Gavin and Liam from west Belfast crowned winners of the BBC's The Big Deal with Steph McGovern.
articles.body:
Two friends from west Belfast, who described themselves as "fish out of water" when it comes to the world of art, have been crowned winners of the BBC's The Big Deal with Steph McGovern

After winning Wednesday's final, Gavin and Liam took home the top prize of £50,000 worth of art.

The show sees budding entrepreneurs battle it out in the world of art dealing, taking on weekly tasks to test their skills, negotiate deals and, most importantly, sell art.

"I'd never been in an art gallery ever and neither had Liam," Gavin said. Adding that it "just shows you can do anything".

Having come into the competition as dark horses, Liam said no-one expected them to even make it to the second round.

He said it was "crazy to watch the evolution from the first episode to the end".

"We're us, we were happy to make it on to the TV and that was about it," he told BBC Radio Ulster's Good Morning Ulster programme.

"But once we got past the first round we began to believe in ourselves a wee bit and the judges saw something in us that we didn't even see."

Gavin added: "A lot of people on the show, I think they came in with an ego like they already knew how to sell art.

"Me and him came in openly admitting we know nothing, but we want to learn."

The final episode saw them pitch a six-figure piece of art at the Frieze Sculpture outdoor exhibition in London's Regent's Park to a group of industry experts.

In true TV style, The contestants were gathered with nothing but a dramatic pause standing between Liam and Gavin and the big win.

"I started to feel sick, and then I started sweating," Gavin said.

"I thought I was going to faint. And then she said, 'Gavin and Liam.'

"I just couldn't believe it. I grabbed Liam and started hugging him. I've never won anything in my life."

Liam said the £50,000 prize was "life-changing money, a life-changing opportunity".

With the win still fresh in their minds, the pair said they have not made any plans about what to spend their winnings on, but the show has spawned a new appreciation for art and owning a new gallery could be on the cards.

Their series mentor Cordelia de Freitas said "there was something in Gavin and Liam that was naïve" when she first met them.

"They were so clearly out of their comfort zone. I thought then and there, 'I can turn them into art dealers'," she said.

"And I didn't even know at that point that they'd never stepped inside an art gallery before."

Presenter Steph McGovern said "week after week" the pair continued to show up and take on "all the advice they were given".

"And it paid off. I'm so proud of them. I can't wait to see what they do next."

articles.title: Soldiers and students study drone technology in Hereford together
articles.summary: The new degree in Hereford combines drone technology, robotics and engineering skills.
articles.body:
Soldiers are swapping military life for university study as part of a new degree designed to prepare the next generation of drone and robotics engineers.

The Autonomous Robotics programme has been developed in partnership with the Army, with military personnel studying alongside civilian students on two and three-year engineering degrees.

The course is being delivered by the New Model Institute for Technology and Engineering (NMITE), a specialist engineering higher education institution in Hereford.

For some of the soldiers taking part, the move from active service to academic life represents a dramatic change of pace.

Thirty-one-year-old Sgt Callum Dervey joined the Army at 18 after leaving school with what he describes as "a few GCSEs".

Now, after 13 years of military service, he has returned to education.

"I'm now back in a cohort of people who are much younger than myself," he said.

"Coming back into an academic setting is certainly already starting to feel challenging, but I'm sure it's going to get easier."

Focusing on autonomous systems, robotics and drone technology, organisers say the course aims to meet growing demand for expertise in emerging technologies.

Military personnel on the programme are taking three-year secondments from active service and are expected to take the skills they develop back into the Army.

Dervey said the Army was looking to increase its engineering expertise and adapt to emerging threats.

"It's so we can adapt rapidly in line with what the current threats are," he said.

"The skills and experience we get from working with academia, industry partners and end users can be taken back and taught to the field Army, which will be crucial in the future."

NMITE president and chief executive James Newby said the degree had been conceived with defence and security in mind, but its applications extended well beyond the military.

"They'll be learning about autonomous systems and robotics and control and mechatronics and systems thinking," he said.

"Those are hugely important skills in manufacturing, agriculture and humanitarian work."

Student Matthew Ryall, who has enrolled on the three-year MEng course, said discussions with lecturers had opened his eyes to the range of careers available.

"It's expanded so much that it could be anything, whether it's manufacturing, defence, whether it's in the air, on the ground or underwater as well," he said.

articles.title: In 1973, a California homeowner paid $5,000 for a city-permitted backyard pool; 53 years later, a sanitation district says it must go as the 29-property easement dispute heads to trial
articles.summary: US News: In 1973, California homeowner Frank Clarke paid $5,000 for a backyard swimming pool after getting the required city permits. More than five decades la.
articles.body: In 1973, California homeowner Frank Clarke paid $5,000 for a backyard swimming pool after getting the required city permits. More than five decades later, the pool is part of a legal dispute over a sewer easement in Huntington Beach, LA Times reported. The Orange County Sanitation District (OC San) says it needs access to the area, while homeowners say they built their backyard structures with city approval.The dispute involves 29 properties on Rhone Lane, where a 30-foot-wide sewer easement runs through the backyards. The easement contains a 69-inch wastewater pipeline installed in 1959, when much of Huntington Beach was farmland. The pipeline carries roughly 10 million gallons of wastewater daily and is part of the regional sewer system.The dispute has now reached court. In May 2026, an Orange County Superior Court judge denied OC San’s motion, allowing the homeowners’ case over the easement to proceed to trial. Judge Deborah Servino said OC San had arguably shown that the full 30 feet could be needed for equipment during an emergency flow bypass. However, she said the district had not shown that the structures and other objects on the properties were interfering with its full use of the easement as a matter of law.The court decision came after OC San started the Miller-Holder Rhone Lane Sewer Easement Cleanup Project in March 2026. The district says the work is needed to keep the pipeline accessible for maintenance, inspections and future repairs. In July, OC San said the cleanup was about 50% complete.Why homeowners are fighting the easementThe sewer easement was recorded with the County of Orange in the early 1960s. The homes on the affected section of Rhone Lane were built during the 1960s and 1970s.Clarke, who has lived at his home since the early 1970s, installed his swimming pool a few years after buying the property. He said he obtained the necessary city permits and did not realise there was a problem until OC San contacted him.A December 2023 letter from OC San listed structures and other items that homeowners needed to remove from the easement. In Clarke’s backyard, these included the swimming pool, pool equipment, decking, a block wall, wood fencing and landscaping.“To me, somebody should have flagged the construction and said, ‘No, you can’t do it, because you’re on an easement,’” Clarke said. “The communication process should have been better.”OC San says pipeline access is necessaryOC San says the easement needs to remain clear so its workers can safely reach the pipeline. The district says encroachments currently limit its ability to carry out routine and preventive maintenance.The pipeline is almost six feet wide and carries about 10 million gallons of wastewater each day. OC San says the sewer line serves tens of thousands of people and carries wastewater to its reclamation plants for treatment and recycling.The district has also said that the pipeline, installed in 1959, remains an important part of the regional sewer system.“The sewer pipeline within the Miller-Holder Rhone Lane easement serves thousands of residents and plays an essential role in preventing sewage spills and system failures,” OC San said in a statement. “Maintaining clear and safe access to this infrastructure is necessary for worker safety, regulatory compliance and long-term system reliability.”Residents question removal Several homeowners have said they obtained permits for their backyard structures and believed they were following the rules.Andrea and Phillip Rizzo are among those affected. Their backyard has an above-ground pool, a swing and a fire pit. The pool has a ramp for their 19-year-old son, A.J., who has cerebral palsy and uses a wheelchair.Andrea Rizzo said the family had not been told exactly where the sewer pipe was located. “If you judge it according to the manhole, the pipe is somewhere between where the ramp is and the fence is,” she said. “They haven’t told us where the pipe is.”Phillip Rizzo said he would be willing to move the pool while OC San accessed the easement. However, he said the reduced backyard space would make it impossible to put the pool back.“If the pipe’s at the end of its life, then let’s discuss it when the pipe’s scheduled to be replaced,” he said. “If it’s replaced in 2025, then give us until 2025 to remove the alleged encroachments.”Some homeowners have settledOC San said agreements were in place with owners of 13 of the 29 properties. The district has continued work at properties where homeowners signed settlement agreements, while other residents remain involved in the litigation.Scott Monastra, whose pool is due to be demolished, signed an agreement in 2024. After the May court ruling, he asked OC San to pause the planned work at his property. The district replied that the ruling did not affect work covered by his agreement.Monastra said OC San representatives came to his home and planned to remove structures, including a covered patio that he had paid to install. The patio was to be dismantled and stored beside his house.“I’m so happy for the guys that didn’t sign the agreement, so they can keep continuing to fight this,” Monastra said. “I hate to use the word, but we caved. I could see how much the fight was going to cost. It’s just a frustrating situation.”The homeowners’ case is now headed towards trial, while OC San continues its cleanup project at the affected properties.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Deadly US strike on Iran school may have been a war crime, UN report finds
articles.summary: Two deadly US strikes on Iran during the opening salvo of the war, including one that hit an elementary school, may have been war crimes, a United Nations investigation concluded in a new report.
articles.body: Two deadly US strikes on Iran during the opening salvo of the war, including one that hit an elementary school, may have been war crimes, a United Nations investigation concluded in a new report. At least 156 people, including 120 children and 26 teachers, were killed when the school in the southern city of Minab was struck on February 28, according to Iranian officials. While there have been slight variances in the reported death toll, it would be considered one of the worst civilian casualty incidents in recent US military history. The UN investigators also examined a second US strike on the same day, which hit a sports center and residential area in the southern city of Lamerd. The strike killed 22 civilians, according to the UN. In both strikes, investigators “found reasonable grounds to believe the United States committed the war crime of launching indiscriminate attacks resulting in the loss of life or injury to civilians or damage to civilian objects,” said the UN’s Independent International Fact-Finding Mission. A US State Department official told CNN that the Trump administration did not find the report credible. They pointed out that President Donald Trump had formally withdrawn the US from the UN Human Rights Council in February 2025, just weeks after he took office, accusing the body of antisemitism. The Department of Defense declined to comment, beyond noting that an investigation was ongoing and it had nothing to announce at the moment. The US has not yet published its own investigation. But early evidence suggests the military accidentally hit the school due to outdated intelligence, as it attacked a neighboring Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps naval base, sources said. The UN report was compiled by a team of independent investigators who analyzed satellite imagery, video and photos, information from credible organizations and experts, and conducted dozens of interviews both in and outside Iran. Their findings will be submitted to the UN Human Rights Council. The UN report also analyzed Iran’s repression of anti-government protesters in late 2025 and early 2026, before the war with the US kicked off. The brutal crackdown killed thousands of people, while detainees were tortured and “disappeared” without notification to their families, it found. These “gross violations amount to crimes against humanity,” the UN investigators said, describing the crackdown as “a widespread and systematic attack on civilians.” CNN has reached out to Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs for comment. The investigators asked for unhindered access to Iran, which the Iranian government did not grant. Of all the UN’s information requests, Iran only responded to about a quarter, the report said. They also requested meetings with US government officials, and information from the Israeli government, which went unanswered. While the US is not a member of the International Criminal Court, the global body that investigates war crimes, it does have its own war crime laws. The school strike US Central Command created target coordinates for the strike that hit the Shajareh Tayyiba school in Minab using outdated information provided by the Defense Intelligence Agency, which contributed to the mistake, two sources briefed on the preliminary findings of the ongoing internal investigation told CNN in March. Satellite imagery from 2013 showed that the school and the IRGC base were once part of the same compound. But images from 2016 revealed that a fence had been erected to separate the school from the rest of the base, and that a separate entrance to the school had been built. Imagery from December 2025 showed dozens of people in the school’s courtyard, apparently playing. “No information indicates that the school was used for military purposes at the time,” the UN report found. “The US failed in its obligation to do everything feasible to verify that it was a military objective.” Trump had initially asserted that Iran might be to blame for the strike, though when pressed on why no one in his own administration seemed to be publicly supporting that claim, he responded: “Because I just don’t know enough about it.” But the Pentagon’s internal investigation has been stuck in limbo for months. The first two stages of a standard investigation were completed within a week of the strike – answering basic questions about whether the strike had hit the intended target, and determining that the US was responsible. But the third stage, where Defense Intelligence Agency analysts review satellite imagery and other intelligence sources, has not yet been ordered by the Pentagon, three sources familiar with the matter told CNN in July. That review would typically provide a more holistic determination about what took place and how a strike impacted the broader mission, and would almost always be conducted in the immediate aftermath of a noteworthy strike, they said. Another independent investigation was separately launched, which included interviews with military service members involved in the strike. But any information gleaned from those interviews has been “locked down” by US Central Command with only a handful of officers permitted access to the details, sources said. CNN previously reported that senior US military commanders bypassed warnings in critical databases that intelligence about potential targets in Iran was severely out of date and went ahead with approving strikes – including one that hit the school.
